cat=cs.CL url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12004v1
s[0] Understanding the Effectiveness of Very Large Language Models on Dialog Evaluation Very Large Language Models for Dialog Evaluation J.
s[1] Huynh et al.
s[2] Jessica Huynh Carnegie Mellon University, jhuynh@cs.cmu.edu Cathy Jiao Carnegie Mellon University, cljiao@cs.cmu.edu Prakhar Gupta Carnegie Mellon University, prakharg@cs.cmu.edu Shikib Mehri Amazon, asmehri@amazon.com (work done while at Carnegie Mellon University) Payal Bajaj Microsoft Turing, pabajaj@microsoft.com Vishrav Chaudhary Microsoft Turing,
s[3] vchaudhary@microsoft.com Maxine Eskenazi Carnegie Mellon University, max@cs.cmu.edu * Jessica Huynh, Cathy Jiao, Prakhar Gupta, Shikib Mehri, Payal Bajaj, Vishrav Chaudhary, Maxine Eskenazi January 14, 2024 =========================================================================================================== Language models have steadily increased in size over the past few years.
s[4] They achieve a high level of performance on various natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as question answering and summarization.
s[5] Large language models (LLMs) have been used for generation and can now output human-like text.
s[6] Due to this, there are other downstream tasks in the realm of dialog that can now harness the LLMs' language understanding capabilities.
s[7] Dialog evaluation is one task that this paper will explore.
s[8] It concentrates on prompting with LLMs: BLOOM, OPT, GPT-3, Flan-T5, InstructDial and TNLGv2.
s[9] The paper shows that the choice of datasets used for training a model contributes to how well it performs on a task as well as on how the prompt should be structured.
s[10] Specifically, the more diverse and relevant the group of datasets that a model is trained on, the better dialog evaluation performs.
s[11] This paper also investigates how the number of examples in the prompt and the type of example selection used affect the model's performance.
s[12] § INTRODUCTION In recent years, language models such as GPT-3 <cit.> have grown larger, and their performance on downstream natural language processing (NLP) tasks has significantly improved in low-resource settings where only a few instances per task are available (few-shot).
s[13] The larger these models are, the higher their performances trend on tasks such as language generation and evaluation <cit.>.
s[14] They can generate coherent, fluent and interesting responses.
s[15] However, they can also produce responses that are repetitive and un-engaging <cit.>, in addition to being hard to control.

READ 2303.15078v3 | Large Language Models are Diverse Role-Players for Summarization Evaluation

s[0] N.
s[1] Wu et al.
s[2] STCA Search & Distribution Group, Microsoft, China wuning,migon,lisho,shiningliang,djiang@microsoft.com Large Language Models are Diverse Role-Players for Summarization Evaluation Ning Wu Ming GongCorresponding author.
s[3] Linjun Shou Shining Liang Daxin Jiang ================================================================================ Text summarization has a wide range of applications in many scenarios.
s[4] The evaluation of the quality of the generated text is a complex problem.
s[5] A big challenge to language evaluation is that there is a clear divergence between existing metrics and human evaluation.
s[6] A document summary’s quality can be assessed by human annotators on various criteria, both objective ones like grammar and correctness, and subjective ones like informativeness, succinctness, and appeal.
s[7] Most of the automatic evaluation methods like BLUE/ROUGE may be not able to adequately capture the above dimensions.
s[8] In this paper, we propose a new evaluation framework based on LLMs, which provides a comprehensive evaluation framework by comparing generated text and reference text from both objective and subjective aspects.
s[9] First, we propose to model objective and subjective dimensions of generated text based on roleplayers prompting mechanism.
s[10] Furthermore, we introduce a context-based prompting mechanism that is able to generate dynamic roleplayer profiles based on input context.
s[11] Finally, we design a multi-roleplayer prompting technology based on batch prompting and integrate multiple outputs into the final evaluation results.
s[12] Experimental results on three real datasets for summarization show that our model is highly competitive and has a very high consistency with human annotators.
s[13] § INTRODUCTION Text summarization has wide applications in various research and application fields.
s[14] Recently, some works found that there is a clear gap between existed metrics like BLEU <cit.>, ROUGE, BertScore <cit.> and human annotations <cit.>.
s[15] Although typical overlap-based and model-based metrics can capture lexicon level or semantic level similarity between generated text and reference text, specific dimensions like coherence, grammar, and interestingness still can't be captured.

cat=cs.CL url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.11916v3
s[0] [ [ January 14, 2024 ==================== In recent years, pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable efficiency in achieving an inference-time few-shot learning capability known as in-context learning.
s[1] However, existing literature has highlighted the sensitivity of this capability to the selection of few-shot demonstrations.
s[2] Current understandings of the underlying mechanisms by which this capability arises from regular language model pretraining objectives remain disconnected from the real-world LLMs.
s[3] This study aims to examine the in-context learning phenomenon through a Bayesian lens, viewing real-world LLMs as latent variable models.
s[4] On this premise, we propose an algorithm to select optimal demonstrations from a set of annotated data with a small LM, and then directly generalize the selected demonstrations to larger LMs.
s[5] We demonstrate significant improvement over baselines, averaged over eight GPT models on eight real-world text classification datasets.
s[6] We also demonstrate the real-world usefulness of our algorithm on GSM8K, a math word problem dataset.
s[7] Our empirical findings support our hypothesis that LLMs implicitly infer a latent variable containing task information.
s[8] [Code: <https://github.com/WANGXinyiLinda/concept-based-demonstration-selection>.] § INTRODUCTION Transformer-based <cit.> pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated significant advancements in a variety of natural language processing (NLP) tasks.
s[9] As the size of these LLMs increases, they gain “in-context learning” capabilities, whereby the models achieve state-of-the-art (SOTA) or near-SOTA performance by conditioning on a small number of demonstration examples at inference time, without any need for updating model parameters <cit.>.
s[10] Below is an example input sequence for semantic analysis with in-context learning: The first two lines are two demonstrations, and the third line is a test input.
s[11] We expect an LLM to output the correct label as a continuation.
s[12] In-context learning has been demonstrated to be an effective technique for a wide range of NLP tasks.
s[13] However, it is sensitive to the choice, format, and even the order of the demonstrations used <cit.>.
s[14] This makes achieving optimal performance with in-context learning a significant challenge, requiring real human effort to adjust the format and selection of demonstration examples.
s[15] Heuristic solutions, such as selecting demonstrations based on the similarity between the demonstrations and test input <cit.> have been proposed, but a comprehensive understanding of why certain demonstrations are effective while others are not remains elusive.

cat=cs.CL url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12832v2
s[0] Large Language Models' Capacity for Augmenting Cross-Domain Analogical Creativity]Fluid Transformers and Creative Analogies: Exploring Large Language Models' Capacity for Augmenting Cross-Domain Analogical Creativity College of Information Studies, University of Maryland USA College of Information Studies, University of Maryland USA Computer and Information Sciences, Temple University USA College of Information Studies, University of Maryland USA Cross-domain analogical reasoning is a core creative ability that can be challenging for humans.
s[1] Recent work has shown some proofs-of-concept of Large language Models’ (LLMs) ability to generate cross-domain analogies.
s[2] However, the reliability and potential usefulness of this capacity for augmenting human creative work has received little systematic exploration.
s[3] In this paper, we systematically explore LLMs capacity to augment cross-domain analogical reasoning.
s[4] Across three studies, we found: 1) LLM-generated cross-domain analogies were frequently judged as helpful in the context of a problem reformulation task (median 4 out of 5 helpfulness rating), and frequently (∼80% of cases) led to observable changes in problem formulations, and 2) there was an upper bound of ∼25% of outputs being rated as potentially harmful, with a majority due to potentially upsetting content, rather than biased or toxic content.
s[5] These results demonstrate the potential utility — and risks — of LLMs for augmenting cross-domain analogical creativity.

s[8] § INTRODUCTION Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 are attracting attention in the creativity research community for their potential to augment creative work by generating tailored design materials and prototypes.
s[9] For example, researchers have explored the potential of LLMs to replicate or assist creative writing tasks such as metaphor generation <cit.>, science writing <cit.> and storytelling <cit.>.
s[10] This research thread parallels explorations in industry, such as the “AI Dungeon" startup's use of GPT-3 to assist with world-building in Dungeons and Dragons <cit.>, prototype systems for AI-assisted content creation[https://www.regie.ai/, https://www.copy.ai/, https://writer.com/] and writing assistance[https://www.compose.ai/], as well as other applications outside of creative writing, such as Q&A conversation[https://chat.openai.com/chat] and code generation[https://github.com/features/copilot].
s[11] Here, we are particularly interested in probing the potential of LLMs to augment cross-domain analogical creativity.
s[12] Cross-domain analogical reasoning is the core cognitive ability to perceive and reason about deep structural similarities between situations that may differ on many surface details <cit.>; for example, using analogy, people can recognize a strong similarity between the solar system and the atom in terms of relational similarity (both involve a central mass — sun, nucleus — orbited by smaller bodies — planets, electrons), ignoring other surface dissimilarities such as their relative size and color.
s[13] Cross-domain analogy is a frequent source of creative breakthroughs, enabling creators to develop powerful new concepts <cit.> or reformulations of their creative problems <cit.>.
s[14] As an illustrative example, Dorst <cit.> reported a case study of how designers used an analogy to a music festival to (re)frame the problem of night violence in King's Cross from a crime prevention / reduction problem with a new entertainment perspective.
s[15] We are motivated by the potential of LLMs to augment creative analogy-making because cross-domain analogies can be hard for humans to retrieve in the creative process.
